evidence: Plaut. Amph. 364: quid nōmen tibi est?
terms.comment: “My name is Mark” is mihi nōmen est Mārcus, or Mārcō, the name in the dative beside mihi: cui Serviō Tulliō fuit nōmen (Liv. 1.39.1).
Quī vocāris?, what are you called?; vocor, my name is.

evidence: Caes. BG 1.1: quī ipsōrum linguā Celtae, nostrā Gallī appellantur
terms.comment: With two accusatives, as in Livy.

evidence: Cic. Amic. 26: amor enim, ex quō amīcitia nōmināta est
Plaut. Men. 263: huic urbī nōmen Epidamnō inditumst
terms.comment: With a dative of the one named; not nōmen dare (below).
A false friend: classically to enrol, above all for military service (Lewis & Short), not to name a child or a pet.

evidence: Lewis & Short: “mostly ante-class. and post-Aug.; esp. in jurid. lang.”

phrases.latin: Quid ais? quid nōmen tibi est? — Sōsiam vocant Thēbānī, Dāvō prōgnātum patre.
phrases.english: What’s that? What’s your name? — The Thebans call me Sosia, son of Davus.

phrases.latin: avicula … est parva, nōmen est cassīta
phrases.english: There is a little bird; its name is cassita, the crested lark.
Oh no, I’ve forgotten the name.

phrases.latin: lūdat lascīva … et nōmen blaesō garriat ōre meum
phrases.english: let her play, full of fun, … and prattle my name with her lisping mouth
